<reason>Both sides were sharp, terse and well grounded in ordinary basin knowledge, and A's framing rhetoric ("delayed light can wait a season; missing Nile flow cannot", "a license to spend the desert's last buffer on an unsigned clock") was the most memorable writing in the debate. But B built the cleaner path to the motion as written. B correctly identified that the proposition is a default-authority question — absent a referee or a signature, someone's calendar governs — and pressed it relentlessly, showing that A's "agreed constraints" collapses into a renewable objection with no off-switch. B's Q2 (would the binding rule ever run downhill: mandatory Aswan drawdown, limits on reclamation?) was the best-aimed question of the round; A answered "yes, both ways", which B fairly converted into the charge that unsigned obligations are enforced only uphill, and A's reply ("unsigned paper binds nobody twice") edges toward conceding that no signature-based constraint blocks Ethiopia at all. B also bit the bullet honestly at the crucial moment ("Ethiopia proceeds... Egypt's objection alone does not stop the clock — that is precisely the motion, and I defend it"), backed by the drought-slows-filling and turbine-throughput mechanisms plus the Aswan buffer and staged-filling record. A did real damage — the distinction between operation (water passes) and filling (water is withheld) was clean, the "cooperating seasons" answer blunted the empirical filling point, the evaporation ledger was correctly reframed as a decades-scale benefit, and "generation is the motive to hold, not a safeguard" was a genuine puncture of B's turbine argument that B never answered in closing. A also narrowed usefully to "a hold on the drought, not a ban on the dam," which partly escapes the wall/veto caricature. Still, A never supplied any trigger, decider, or mechanism for that hold, leaving B's who-decides question live at the end. Minor demerit for B claiming "no answer came" to its Q2 before A had a chance to reply, though B fairly corrected that in closing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Q2 and its follow-through: asking whether the binding constraint would ever run downstream (Aswan drawdown, reclamation limits) forced A to concede a two-way rule that Egypt has never accepted, letting B show that A's "agreed constraints" enforces unsigned obligations only against the upstream state — the 1959 allocation in cooperation vocabulary. A's best counter-punch was that a hydropower dam's incentive during filling is to hold water, not release it, which undercut B's "turbines need throughput" answer and went unanswered in B's closing.</best_rebuttal>
